DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Priority
Receipt is acknowledged of certified copies of papers required by 37 CFR 1.55.
Drawings
The drawings are objected to under 37 CFR 1.83(a).  The drawings must show every feature of the invention specified in the claims.  Therefore, the “a wall, wherein the wall at least partially encloses a side of the seat when the seat is in the first position, the wall thereby blocking access to the seat from an aisle when in the first position, and wherein the wall does not enclose the side of the seat when the seat is in the second position so that a passenger can access the seat from an aisle when the seat is in the second position” must be shown or the feature(s) canceled from the claim(s).  No new matter should be entered.
Corrected drawing sheets in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment of the application. Any amended replacement drawing sheet should include all of the figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet, even if only one figure is being amended. The figure or figure number of an amended drawing should not be labeled as “amended.” If a drawing figure is to be canceled, the appropriate figure must be removed from the replacement sheet, and where necessary, the remaining figures must be renumbered and appropriate changes made to the brief description of the several views of the drawings for consistency. Additional replacement sheets may be necessary to show the renumbering of the remaining figures. Each drawing sheet submitted after the filing date of an application must be labeled in the top margin as either “Replacement Sheet” or “New Sheet” pursuant to 37 CFR 1.121(d). If the changes are not accepted by the examiner, the applicant will be notified and informed of any required corrective action in the next Office action. The objection to the drawings will not be held in abeyance.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 6-9, 17, and 18 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor (or for applications subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, the applicant), regards as the invention.
Regarding claim 6, claim 6 recites the limitations the first position and “the second position” in lines 3, 4, 5 and 6.  There is insufficient antecedent basis for these limitations in the claim.
Additionally, the limitation “wherein the wall at least partially encloses a side of the seat when the seat is in the first position, the wall thereby blocking access to the seat from an aisle when in the first position, and wherein the wall does not enclose the side of the seat when the seat is in the second position so that a passenger can access the seat from an aisle when the seat is in the second position” is indefinite because it is unclear how the wall can block access to the seat when the seat is an upright (first) position, but not when the seat is in a lie flat (second) position. Applicant is encouraged to amend and provide arguments so as to explain or clarify the scope of this claim. This claim can not be understood as written.
Regarding claim 7, claim 7 recites the limitation “the second position” in lines 5 and 6.  There is insufficient antecedent basis for these limitations in the claim.
Regarding claim 17, the limitation “A shell suitable for use as the shell of claim 10, wherein the shell comprises a movable panel, a footrest, and a console” is indefinite because there is unclear dependency on claim 10 and it appears that there is double inclusion of the movable panel, footrest, and console. This claim is being interpreted as not being dependent on claim 10.
Regarding claim 18, the limitation “A kit of parts configured such that when assembled, the kit of parts forms an aircraft passenger seat unit as defined in claim 1” is indefinite as it is unclear what is meant by ‘kit.’ Does the kit consist of unassembled parts for passenger seat unit or tools for assembling the seat unit? In the former case, the limitation would be met by the seat unit of claim 1. In the latter case appears to be insufficient disclosure in the specification to explain what would be required. This is being interpreted as the kit consisting of parts that would form the aircraft passenger seat when assembled. In other words, the ‘kit of parts’ is never defined. What parts are in the kit? As such, it is unclear to the meets and bounds.
Claims 6-10 and 17 are rejected for being dependent on a rejected claim.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis (i.e., changing from AIA  to pre-AIA ) for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(a)(1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
(a)(2) the claimed invention was described in a patent issued under section 151, or in an application for patent published or deemed published under section 122(b), in which the patent or application, as the case may be, names another inventor and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
Claim(s) 1-2, 4-5, 6 (as best understood), 7-10, and 17 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by Nicholas (US 10501188 B2).
Regarding claim 1, Nicholas (US 10501188 B2) discloses an aircraft passenger seat unit (Nicholas, figures 7a-d, item 709), configured for use adjacent an aisle of an aircraft cabin (Nicholas, figures 1e and 7a-d, item 111, seat units adjacent aircraft aisle), wherein the seat unit comprises:
- a seat (Nicholas, figure 7a-d, item 709),
- a footrest (Nicholas, figure 7b, item 726), and
- a movable panel (Nicholas, figure 7a-d, item 725, end wall made of a panel moves), movable with respect to the footrest between a closed position in which the movable panel at least partially encloses a side of the footrest (Nicholas, figure 7a, item 725, panel in closed configuration enclosing a side of the footrest) and an open position in which the movable panel at least partially exposes the side of the footrest such that, in use, when the panel is in the open position, a passenger can access the seat from an aisle through the partially exposed side of the footrest (Nicholas, figure 7c, item 725, panel in open configuration exposing a side of the footrest and thereby allowing passenger access to the footrest from the aisle).
Regarding claim 2, Nicholas discloses an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 1,
wherein the seat comprises a seat pan (Nicholas, figure 7a, item 715b) and backrest (Nicholas, figure 7a, item 715a),
the seat having an upright sitting configuration in which the backrest is substantially upright (Nicholas, figure 7a, item 715a, seat in upright position where backrest is upright), and
wherein the seat is movable in the upright sitting configuration between a first position in which the seat pan is spaced apart from the footrest by a first distance (Nicholas, figures 7a-b, items 715b and 726, forward seat has seat pan and footrest spaced apart by a distance), and a second position in which the seat pan is spaced apart from the footrest by a second distance, the second distance being less than the first distance (Nicholas, figure 7a-b, item 715b and 726, aft seat has seat spaced apart from footrest by a distance less than the first distance).
Regarding claim 4, Nicholas discloses an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 2, wherein the seat faces in a direction defining a seat axis, and wherein the seat is movable along the seat axis towards or away from the footrest when the seat is moved between the first and second positions (Nicholas, figure 7a, item 709, col 13 lines 10-22, forwards and aftwards seats move along an axis between a first and second position).
Regarding claim 5, Nicholas discloses an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 1, wherein the seat unit has an aisle side that is configured to be adjacent an aisle in use (Nicholas, figure 7a, item 733, side of seat unit has an opening designed to be adjacent to aisle for allowing passengers access to the seat unit), and
wherein the movable panel is positioned along the aisle side of the seat unit when in the closed position such that movable panel at least partially encloses the side of the footrest to block access to the side of the footrest from the aisle, and such that when the panel is in the open position a passenger can access the at least partially exposed side of the footrest from the aisle (Nicholas, figures 7a and 7c, item 725, panel positioned along the aisle side of the seat unit blocks or allows access to the footwell directly from the aisle, depending upon whether closed or opened).
Regarding claim 6 (as best understood), Nicholas discloses an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 1 further comprising a wall (Nicholas, figure 7a-b, item 727, side wall),
wherein the wall at least partially encloses a side of the seat when the seat is in the first position (Nicholas, figure 7a-b, item 727, wall partially encloses seat unit when seat is in the upright position),
Regarding claim 7, Nicholas discloses an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 6, wherein the movable panel and wall are spaced apart along a first side of the seat unit and the space between the movable panel and wall defines an access path that provides passenger access into the seat unit from the first side of the seat unit (Nicholas, figures 7b and 7d, item 733, access path between the wall and the panel), and wherein the seat is adjacent to the access path when in the second position so that a passenger can access the seat from a first side of the seat unit via the access path when the seat is in the second position (Nicholas, figures 7b and 7d, items 715 and 733, access path between the wall and the panel allows access to the seat when the seat is in upright position).
Regarding claim 8, Nicholas discloses an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 6, wherein the seat unit comprises a console (Nicholas, figure 7a, item 737, base forming part of the console) comprising a table surface for use by a passenger of the seat unit (Nicholas, figure 7a, item 729, table surface) and wherein the console is at least partially formed by the wall (Nicholas, figure 7a, item 727, side wall forming part of console).
Regarding claim 9, Nicholas discloses an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 8, wherein the aircraft passenger seat unit is configured to be positioned directly adjacent to and in front of a further, substantially identical aircraft seat unit (Nicholas, figure 7c, item 709, seat units positioned on in front of the other), and wherein the console is at least partially formed by the movable panel of the further seat unit (Nicholas, figure 7a, item 725, movable panel of one seat unit forms part of the console of the forward seat unit).
Regarding claim 10, Nicholas discloses an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 9. further comprising a shell, wherein the shell forms the console of the seat unit and the movable panel of the further seat unit (Nicholas, figure 7a, items 725, 727, and 737, console forms a shell structure around the seat unit).
Regarding claim 17, Nicholas discloses a shell suitable for use as the shell of claim 10, wherein the shell comprises
a movable panel (Nicholas, figure 7a-d, item 725, end wall made of a panel moves),
a footrest (Nicholas, figure 7b, item 726), and
a console (Nicholas, figure 7a, item 737, base forming part of the console),
wherein the movable panel and footrest are suitable for forming the movable panel and footrest of a first seat unit (Nicholas, figure 7a-d, item 709, shell used as part of seat unit), the movable panel being movable with respect to the footrest between a closed position in which the movable panel at least partially encloses a side of the footrest at a first side of the shell (Nicholas, figure 7a, item 725, panel in closed configuration enclosing a side of the footrest) and an open position in which the panel at least partially exposes the side of the footrest at the first side of the shell (Nicholas, figure 7c, item 725, panel in open configuration exposing a side of the footrest and thereby allowing passenger access to the footrest from the aisle), and
wherein the console is suitable for forming the console of a second, directly adjacent seat unit, and wherein the movable panel at least partially forms the console (Nicholas, figure 7a, see callout below, console forms part of console of forward seat unit).

Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
The text of those sections of Title 35, U.S. Code not included in this action can be found in a prior Office action.
The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention(s) absent any evidence to the contrary.  Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and effective filing dates of each claim that was not commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the later invention in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) for any potential 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) prior art against the later invention.
Claim(s) 3 and 18 (as best understood) is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Nicholas (US 10501188 B2) as applied to claim 1 above.
Regarding claim 3, Nicholas discloses an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 2, except:
wherein the second distance is no more than 15 centimeters.
However, Nicholas shows a second distance having a dimension that is in a similar range to the claimed range (<=15 cm) and the second distance has inherent dimensions.
The applicant has not established criticality for the second distance being less than 15 cm, It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the second distance to be less than 15 cm in order to prevent an occupant’s feet from fitting between the seat and the footrest, since it has been held that where the general conditions of a claim are disclosed in the prior art, discovering the optimum or workable ranges involves only routine skill in the art.  In re Aller, 105 USPQ 233.
Regarding claim 18 (as best understood), Nicholas discloses the aircraft passenger seat unit as defined in claim 1, except:
a kit of parts configured such that when assembled, the kit of parts forms an aircraft passenger seat unit as defined in claim 1.
Nicholas discloses the aircraft passenger seat unit as defined in claim 1 discloses the claimed invention except for a kit of parts that, when assembled, the kit of parts forms an aircraft passenger seat unit as defined in claim.  It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have a kit of separate parts for forming the seat unit in order to allow the seat unit to be assembled in an aircraft with small doors where the fully assembled seat unit would not fit through doors, since it has been held that constructing a formerly integral structure in various elements involves only routine skill in the art.  Nerwin v. Erlichman, 168 USPQ 177, 179.
Claim(s) 11 and 13 are is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Nicholas (US 10501188 B2) as applied to claim 1 above, and further in view of Pethier (US 11794902 B2).
Regarding claim 11, Nicholas teaches an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 1, except:
wherein the movable panel is movably mounted via a hinge.
Pethier (US 11794902 B2) teaches a movable panel which is movably mounted via a hinge (Pethier, figure 3, item 86, hinge which mounts movable panel).
Nicholas and Pethier are both considered analogous art as they are both in the same field of aircraft personnel accommodations. It would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the application for one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the movable panel of Nicholas with the panel and hinge allowing horizontal movement of Pethier with a reasonable expectation of success in order to reduce the disruption to other the access opening of other seats.
Regarding claim 13, Nicholas as modified by Pethier teaches an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 11, wherein the movable panel is mounted via a hinge and configured to be moved between the closed position and open position about a vertical axis located towards a side of the panel (Pethier, figure 3, item 86, hinge which mounts movable panel allows the panel to move a bout a vertical axis between an opened and closed position).
Claim(s) 11 and 12 are is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Nicholas (US 10501188 B2) in view of Pethier (US 11794902 B2) as applied to claim 1 above, and further in view of Guering (US 20130126671 A1).
Regarding claim 11, Nicholas teaches an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 1, except:
wherein the movable panel is movably mounted via a hinge.
Guering (US 20130126671 A1) teaches a movable panel which is movably mounted via a hinge (Guering, figures 5-8, items 20 and 38, movable panel mounted via hinge).
Nicholas and Guering are both considered analogous art as they are both in the same field of aircraft personnel accommodations. It would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the application for one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the movable panel of Nicholas with the panel and hinge allowing vertical movement of Guering with a reasonable expectation of success in order to in order to reduce the disruption to other the access opening of other seats.
Regarding claim 12, Nicholas as modified by Guering teaches an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 11,
wherein the movable panel is mounted via a hinge and configured to be moved between the closed position and open position about a horizontal axis located towards a bottom of the panel (Guering, figures 5-8, items 20 and 38, hinge allowing movable panel to be moved between the open and closed position about a horizontal axis which is located at the panel bottom).
Claim(s) 14-16 are is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Nicholas (US 10501188 B2) as applied to claim 1 above, and further in view of Robinson (US 20170283064 A1).
Regarding claim 14, Nicholas teaches an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 1, wherein the seat unit comprises a locking system configured to lock the movable panel in the closed position (Nicholas, col 13 lines 28-35, panel releasably locked in place), the lock system comprising:
- a latch positioned configured to engage to lock the movable panel in the closed position (Nicholas, col 13 lines 28-35, latch locks the movable panel in the closed position), except:
wherein the locking system comprises a plurality of latches positioned on the movable panel and configured to engage with a structure of the seat unit or vice verse to lock the movable panel in the closed position.
Robinson (US 20170283064 A1) teaches a movable panel locking system;
wherein the locking system comprises a plurality of latches (Robinson, figure 6, item 56 and 72, latches) positioned on the movable panel and configured to engage with a structure of the seat unit or vice verse to lock the movable panel in the closed position (Robinson, figure 3, items 34a and 32, latches attached to movable panel engage with seat unit structure locks the movable panel closed).
Nicholas and Robinson are both considered analogous art as they are both in the same field of aircraft passenger accommodations. It would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the application for one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the invention of Nicholas with the locking system including multiple latches of Robinson with a reasonable expectation of success in order to provide redundancy to prevent panels from moving to the open position when undesired.
Regarding claim 15, Nicholas as modified by Robinson teaches an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 14, wherein the lock system comprises an actuatable member operable to disengage the latches so that the movable panel can be moved from the closed position to the open position (Robinson, figures 6 and 7a, item 58, 60, 74, latch controls disengage latches).
Regarding claim 16, Nicholas as modified by Robinson teaches an aircraft passenger seat unit according to claim 15, wherein the actuatable member is positioned on a surface of the movable panel that is adjacent the footrest when the panel is in the closed position (Robinson, figures 6 and 7a, latch controls are positioned on the panel; Nicholas, figure 7a-d, item 725, wall panel is adjacent to the footrest).
Conclusion
The prior art made of record and not relied upon is considered pertinent to applicant's disclosure.
Davis (US 11299274 B1) teaches a movable panel but for the seat rather than the footrest
Dowty (US 11345476 B2) teaches a movable panel between seats that seems to obstruct footrest when closed
Katakura (US 11731764 B2) teaches a movable armrest for the seat
Wallace (US 20130241258 A1) teaches a moveable door panel
Henshaw (US 9469405 B2) teaches a seat with a movable panel
